Name: {{PATIENT_NAME}}                Unit No: {{MRN}}

Service: MEDICINE
Allergies: Penicillin (rash)
Attending: {{PROVIDER_1}}

Chief Complaint:
Fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath

Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
None

History of Present Illness:
78-year-old {{SEX}} w/ h/o Parkinson's disease with a parkinsonian gait, HTN, and prior aspiration events presenting with 4 days of productive cough, subjective fevers to 101.5F, and progressive SOB. Reports decreased PO intake and one episode of choking while eating. In the ED, febrile to 38.9, tachypneic to 26, satting 88% on RA and improved to 94% on 3L NC. CXR showed RLL consolidation. {{PATIENT_REF}} was started on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin for CAP with aspiration risk.

Past Medical History:
1. Parkinson's disease with parkinsonian gait
2. Hypertension
3. Hyperlipidemia
4. GERD
5. Prior aspiration pneumonia

Social History:
Former smoker, 20 pack-years, quit 15 yrs ago. No EtOH. Lives at {{ADDRESS}} with spouse who assists with ADLs. Retired teacher. Ambulates with a walker.

Physical Exam:
ADMISSION:
VS: T 38.9 HR 98 BP 142/84 RR 26 SpO2 88% RA
Gen: elderly, mild resp distress
CV: RRR, no m/r/g
Pulm: crackles RLL, decreased BS at right base
Abd: soft, NT/ND
Neuro: resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, masked facies
Ext: no edema

DISCHARGE:
VS: T 37.0 HR 76 BP 128/78 RR 18 SpO2 95% RA
Pulm: improved air movement, scattered crackles RLL
Gen: comfortable, no distress

Pertinent Results:
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: WBC 15.8 Hgb 12.9 Plt 288
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Na 134 K 4.3 Cl 99 HCO3 24 BUN 22 Cr 1.0 Glu 118
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Lactate 1.8, Procalcitonin 2.4
{{DISCHARGE_DATE}}: WBC 9.1 Hgb 12.5 Plt 301

Brief Hospital Course:
78-year-old with Parkinson's disease admitted for community-acquired pneumonia with aspiration risk. WBC peaked at 15.8 on {{ADMIT_DATE}} and downtrended to 9.1 by discharge. Blood cultures NGTD. Transitioned from IV ceftriaxone/azithromycin to PO amoxicillin-clavulanate after 48h with clinical improvement, afebrile and weaning off supplemental O2. SLP evaluated and recommended a soft, nectar-thick diet with aspiration precautions. {{PATIENT_REF}} ambulated with PT and was cleared for discharge home with services.

Medications on Admission:
1. Carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg PO TID
2. Lisinopril 20 mg PO daily
3. Atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily
4. Omeprazole 20 mg PO daily

Discharge Medications:
1. Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875-125 mg PO BID x5 days (NEW)
2. Carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg PO TID
3. Lisinopril 20 mg PO daily
4. Atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily
5. Omeprazole 20 mg PO daily

Discharge Disposition: Home with services

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: Community-acquired pneumonia with aspiration
Secondary: Parkinson's disease, hypertension, GERD

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory with walker

Discharge Instructions:
- Complete the full antibiotic course
- Follow aspiration precautions; soft diet, thickened liquids
- Follow up with {{PROVIDER_2}} on {{APPT_DATE_1}}
- Return for worsening SOB, high fever, or chest pain

Chief Complaint:
Progressive dyspnea on exertion and leg swelling

Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
None

History of Present Illness:
72-year-old {{SEX}} w/ h/o HFrEF (EF 30%), CAD s/p PCI, HTN, and CKD stage 3 presenting with 1 week of worsening DOE, 3-pillow orthopnea, PND, and bilateral LE edema. Reports a 6 lb weight gain and dietary indiscretion at a family event. Denies CP. In the ED, BP 158/92, satting 90% on RA improving on 2L NC, with JVD and bibasilar crackles. Treated with IV furosemide with good diuretic response.

Past Medical History:
1. Heart failure with reduced EF (30%)
2. Coronary artery disease s/p PCI
3. Hypertension
4. CKD stage 3
5. Type 2 diabetes mellitus

Social History:
Never smoker. Rare EtOH. Lives at {{ADDRESS}} independently. Retired accountant. Independent in all ADLs.

Physical Exam:
ADMISSION:
VS: T 36.8 HR 88 BP 158/92 RR 22 SpO2 90% RA
Gen: mild resp distress
CV: RRR, JVP ~12 cm, no murmurs
Pulm: bibasilar crackles
Abd: soft, NT
Ext: 2+ pitting edema to knees bilaterally

DISCHARGE:
VS: T 36.9 HR 74 BP 126/76 RR 16 SpO2 96% RA
CV: JVP ~7 cm
Ext: trace edema

Pertinent Results:
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: WBC 7.2 Hgb 11.8 Plt 210
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Na 136 K 4.0 Cl 101 HCO3 26 BUN 34 Cr 1.6 Glu 152
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: BNP 1840, Troponin <0.01
{{DISCHARGE_DATE}}: Na 138 K 4.2 BUN 30 Cr 1.5

Brief Hospital Course:
72-year-old with HFrEF admitted with an acute decompensated heart failure exacerbation. BNP was 1840 on {{ADMIT_DATE}}, consistent with volume overload. Diuresed with IV furosemide to a net negative 4.2 L over the stay, with creatinine bumping from 1.5 to a peak of 1.6 on {{ADMIT_DATE}} before stabilizing. GDMT was optimized: carvedilol continued and sacubitril-valsartan initiated at a low dose with counseling on daily weights. The patient was euvolemic and ambulating without dyspnea by discharge.

Medications on Admission:
1. Furosemide 40 mg PO daily
2. Carvedilol 12.5 mg PO BID
3. Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily
4. Atorvastatin 80 mg PO daily
5. Metformin 1000 mg PO BID

Discharge Medications:
1. Furosemide 80 mg PO daily (dose increased)
2. Sacubitril-valsartan 24-26 mg PO BID (NEW; lisinopril discontinued)
3. Carvedilol 12.5 mg PO BID
4. Atorvastatin 80 mg PO daily
5. Metformin 1000 mg PO BID

Discharge Disposition: Home

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: Acute decompensated heart failure
Secondary: HFrEF, CAD, CKD stage 3, type 2 diabetes

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory, independent

Discharge Instructions:
- Daily weights; call for a gain of more than 3 lb in 2 days
- Low-sodium (2 g) diet and fluid restriction 2 L/day
- Follow up with cardiology {{PROVIDER_2}} on {{APPT_DATE_1}}
- Follow up with PCP {{PROVIDER_3}} on {{APPT_DATE_2}}
- Return for worsening SOB, chest pain, or lightheadedness

Denies fever or CP. Baseline on 2L home O2. In the ED, satting 86% on RA, tachypneic, with diffuse wheezing; improved after nebs and IV steroids. {{PATIENT_REF}} was admitted for a COPD exacerbation and started on prednisone and azithromycin.

Past Medical History:
1. COPD, GOLD 3
2. Bell's palsy, resolved
3. Hypertension
4. GERD

Current smoker, 40 pack-years, still smoking half PPD. No EtOH. Lives at {{ADDRESS}} with a daughter. On 2L home O2.

VS: T 37.1 HR 96 BP 148/86 RR 24 SpO2 86% RA
Gen: pursed-lip breathing, accessory muscle use
CV: RRR
Pulm: diffuse expiratory wheezes, prolonged expiration
Neuro: symmetric facial movement, no residual palsy
Ext: no edema

VS: T 36.9 HR 80 BP 132/80 RR 18 SpO2 92% on 2L
Pulm: mild scattered wheeze, improved air movement

Pertinent Results:
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: WBC 11.2 Hgb 14.6 Plt 233
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Na 140 K 4.4 Cl 102 HCO3 30 BUN 16 Cr 0.9 Glu 138
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: VBG pH 7.35 pCO2 52
{{DISCHARGE_DATE}}: WBC 8.4 HCO3 29

Brief Hospital Course:
65-year-old with severe COPD admitted for an acute exacerbation. WBC was 11.2 on {{ADMIT_DATE}} with a compensated respiratory acidosis (pCO2 52), consistent with chronic CO2 retention. Treated with scheduled nebulized bronchodilators, a prednisone burst, and a 5-day course of azithromycin. Weaned back to baseline 2L home O2 requirement by discharge. Smoking cessation counseling provided and nicotine replacement offered.

2. Fluticasone-salmeterol 250-50 INH BID
3. Albuterol INH PRN
4. Amlodipine 5 mg PO daily

Discharge Medications:
1. Prednisone 40 mg PO daily x5 days (NEW)
2. Azithromycin 250 mg PO daily x4 more days (NEW)
3. Tiotropium 18 mcg INH daily
4. Fluticasone-salmeterol 250-50 INH BID
5. Albuterol INH PRN
6. Amlodipine 5 mg PO daily

Discharge Disposition: Home

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: COPD exacerbation
Secondary: Chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, hypertension

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory with exertional dyspnea

Discharge Instructions:
- Complete the prednisone and azithromycin courses
- Continue home O2 at 2L; do not increase without guidance
- Follow up with PCP {{RELATIVE_DATE}}
- Return for worsening SOB, confusion, or bluish lips

Chief Complaint:
Black tarry stools and one episode of hematemesis

Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
EGD with epinephrine injection and hemoclip placement

History of Present Illness:
58-year-old {{SEX}} w/ h/o Barrett's esophagus, GERD, and chronic NSAID use for knee OA presenting with 2 days of melena and one episode of coffee-ground emesis. Reports lightheadedness on standing. Denies hematochezia or abdominal pain. In the ED, HR 108, BP 104/66, orthostatic, with Hgb 7.1. {{PATIENT_REF}} received 2 units pRBC and an IV pantoprazole drip, and GI was consulted for urgent EGD.

Past Medical History:
1. Barrett's esophagus
2. GERD
3. Osteoarthritis
4. Hypertension

Social History:
Former smoker, quit 10 yrs ago. Social EtOH, 2-3 drinks/week. Lives at {{ADDRESS}} with spouse. Works as a contractor.

Physical Exam:
ADMISSION:
VS: T 36.7 HR 108 BP 104/66 RR 18 SpO2 98% RA
Gen: pale, anxious
CV: tachycardic, regular
Abd: soft, mild epigastric tenderness, no rebound
Rectal: melena on exam
Ext: cool, no edema

DISCHARGE:
VS: T 36.8 HR 78 BP 122/74 RR 16 SpO2 99% RA
Abd: soft, NT

Pertinent Results:
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: WBC 9.8 Hgb 7.1 Plt 190
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Na 139 K 4.0 Cl 103 HCO3 24 BUN 38 Cr 1.0 Glu 122
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: INR 1.1
{{DISCHARGE_DATE}}: Hgb 9.4 BUN 18

Brief Hospital Course:
58-year-old with Barrett's esophagus admitted with an acute upper GI bleed. Hgb nadir was 7.1 on {{ADMIT_DATE}} and rose to 9.4 after transfusion of 2 units pRBC. EGD revealed a single Forrest IIa gastric ulcer, which was treated with epinephrine injection and hemoclip placement; biopsies were taken and Barrett's surveillance was noted. NSAIDs were discontinued and a high-dose PPI was continued. {{PATIENT_REF}} remained hemodynamically stable with no rebleeding for 48h prior to discharge.

Medications on Admission:
1. Ibuprofen 600 mg PO TID PRN
2. Omeprazole 20 mg PO daily
3. Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily

Discharge Medications:
1. Pantoprazole 40 mg PO BID (NEW, replacing omeprazole)
2. Acetaminophen 650 mg PO Q6H PRN (replacing ibuprofen)
3. Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily

Discharge Disposition: Home

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: Upper GI bleed from gastric ulcer
Secondary: Barrett's esophagus, GERD, acute blood-loss anemia

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory, independent

Discharge Instructions:
- No NSAIDs; use acetaminophen for pain
- Take pantoprazole twice daily before meals
- Follow up with GI {{PROVIDER_2}} on {{APPT_DATE_1}} for biopsy results and Barrett's surveillance planning
- Return for black stools, vomiting blood, dizziness, or fainting

None

34-year-old {{SEX}} w/ h/o type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with 1 day of N/V, diffuse abdominal pain, polyuria, and polydipsia in the setting of a viral URI and missed insulin doses. In the ED, glucose 486, anion gap 22, beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated, and moderate serum ketones, consistent with DKA. Started on IV fluids, an insulin drip, and electrolyte repletion per protocol.

Past Medical History:
1. Type 1 diabetes mellitus
2. Hypothyroidism

Nonsmoker. Occasional EtOH. Lives at {{ADDRESS}} with roommates. Graduate student.

VS: T 36.9 HR 80 BP 116/74 RR 16 SpO2 100% RA

Pertinent Results:
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: WBC 13.4 Hgb 14.1 Plt 265
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Na 132 K 5.2 Cl 98 HCO3 12 BUN 24 Cr 1.2 Glu 486
{{ADMIT_DATE}}: Anion gap 22, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8, VBG pH 7.22
{{DISCHARGE_DATE}}: Na 138 K 4.0 HCO3 24 Glu 168 Anion gap 10

34-year-old with type 1 diabetes admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by a viral illness and insulin nonadherence. The anion gap closed from 22 on {{ADMIT_DATE}} to 10 by {{DISCHARGE_DATE}} on an insulin drip with IV fluids and potassium repletion. Once the gap closed and the patient was tolerating PO, they were transitioned to their home subcutaneous basal-bolus regimen with overlap. Diabetes education reinforced sick-day rules and the importance of not omitting basal insulin.

2. Insulin lispro sliding scale with meals

4. Sertraline 50 mg PO daily
5. Ondansetron 4 mg PO Q8H PRN nausea (NEW)

Primary: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Secondary: Type 1 diabetes mellitus, viral upper respiratory infection

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory, independent

Discharge Instructions:
- Never stop basal insulin, even when not eating
- Check glucose and ketones when ill; hydrate
- Follow up with endocrinology {{PROVIDER_2}} on {{APPT_DATE_1}}

Secondary: Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes, chronic venous insufficiency

Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory, independent

Discharge Instructions:
- Complete the full course of cephalexin
- Elevate the leg; keep the area clean and dry
- Follow up with PCP {{RELATIVE_DATE}}
- Return for spreading redness beyond the marked borders, fever, or drainage

In the ED, HR 112, satting 91% on RA, with a positive Wells score. CTA chest confirmed segmental and subsegmental PEs in the right lower lobe without RV strain. Brief Hospital Course:
67-year-old with a history of non-Hodgkin lymphoma admitted with acute segmental pulmonary embolism. D-dimer was 3.6 on {{ADMIT_DATE}} with a normal troponin and BNP, reassuring against RV strain, and the patient was risk-stratified as low-risk PE. Started on apixaban with a loading dose. Hypoxia resolved and the patient ambulated on room air with stable saturations. Given the prior DVT and malignancy history, hematology was consulted regarding duration of anticoagulation and recommended indefinite therapy pending outpatient review.

1. Amlodipine 10 mg PO daily
2. Atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily

1. Apixaban 10 mg PO BID x7 days, then 5 mg PO BID (NEW)
2. Amlodipine 10 mg PO daily
3. Atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily

Discharge Disposition: Home

Discharge Diagnosis:
Primary: Acute pulmonary embolism
Secondary: History of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, prior DVT, hypertension

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Alert and oriented x3
Level of Consciousness: Alert
Activity Status: Ambulatory, independent

Discharge Instructions:
- Take apixaban exactly as prescribed; do not miss doses
- Avoid activities with a high bleeding risk
- Follow up with hematology/anticoagulation {{PROVIDER_2}} on {{APPT_DATE_1}}
- Follow up with PCP {{PROVIDER_3}} on {{APPT_DATE_2}}
